title: The bird on the 11,000 V line
hook: Birds perch on bare power lines every day. What voltage is across one?

doesNotKnow: that voltage is a difference between two points
that current flows through something only when its two ends sit at different voltages

misconception: A bird on an 11,000 V line has 11,000 V through it and survives only because birds are insulated or lucky.
objective: The learner can explain that voltage is a difference between two points: a bird on one line has almost no voltage between its feet, so almost no current flows through it, but touching the grounded pole puts the full 11,000 V across it.

claims.text: Current through a conductor needs a potential difference across it (I = ΔV / R); reveal: 'Current needs a voltage difference to push it, so almost none goes through the bird.'
claims.source: Ohm's law: any introductory electricity text (e.g. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, chapter 9, Current and Resistance; fact-checker picks the section). Brief: company/domains/briefs/physics.electricity.md round 3 #2, claim 1. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD UNVERIFIED. Read Demo.tsx first: the reveal sentence matches the claim. The claim rests on Ohm's law as stated in an external text (OpenStax UP2 ch. 9). WebFetch failed (DNS) for openstax.org and its mirrors (libretexts, xyzhomework), and curl got a proxy 403. Search snippets only. Not verified: it needs a source that can be opened here, or the evaluation-steward can rule that a basic law may rest on derivation. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED on an opened source: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, section 9.4 'Ohm's Law' (raw GitHub openstax/osbooks-university-physics-bundle, module m58732, opened 2026-10-14): 'the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the voltage applied ... voltage the cause and current the effect' (I = V/R). With about 0.002 V across the bird (c2), almost no current flows, which matches the reveal.

claims.text: On a line at 11,000 V to ground carrying 200 A, each foot reads 11,000 V against ground, and the wire between feet 5 cm apart drops 0.002 V (2 cm: 0.001 V; 20 cm: 0.008 V); stage: 'foot 1–ground' / 'foot 2–ground' meter readings, seen line 'feet–ground 11,000 V', 'across 5 cm 0.002 V'; reveal: '11,000 V from each foot to the ground, and only 0.002 V between them'.
claims.source: ΔV = I R' L with I = 200 A, R' = 0.2 ohm/km: 200 x 0.0002 x 0.05 = 0.002 V (Demo.tsx `acrossV`, shown with toFixed(3); 7 cm gives 0.0028 -> '0.003 V'). Foot 2 reads 11,000 - 0.002 V, shown rounded as 11,000 V. Current and conductor resistance are illustrative (brief claim 2; check.mjs); real line currents and conductors vary. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node port acrossV(cm) = 200 × 0.0002 × cm/100: 5 cm 0.002 V; 2 cm 0.0008 V, which toFixed(3) shows as '0.001 V'; 20 cm 0.008 V. Foot 1 reads V_LINE; foot 2 reads 11,000 − 0.002, which fmtV rounds to '11,000 V'. Seen line 'feet 11,000 V' needs both feet; 'across 5 cm 0.002 V' and the reveal quote the stored across reading (updated by the slider only while in across mode). The 2 cm value is a 3-decimal display of 0.0008 V; the claim says what the stage shows. | v2 (2026-10-14, demo-builder, W-576 learner r9): single-foot readings now name ground: meter 'foot 1–ground' / 'foot 2–ground', seen line 'feet–ground 11,000 V', reveal 'Your voltmeter read 11,000 V from each foot to the ground, and only 0.003 V between them' (QA path at 7 cm). Values unchanged. Previous verdict void; needs re-check. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED (v2). Own node acrossV(cm) = 200 × 0.0002 × cm/100: 5 cm 0.002 V; 2 cm 0.0008 V, shown '0.001 V' by toFixed(3); 7 cm 0.0028 V, shown '0.003 V'; 20 cm 0.008 V. Foot 2 reads 11,000 − 0.002, which fmtV rounds to '11,000 V'. Meter labels 'foot 1–ground' / 'foot 2–ground', seen line '{feet}–ground 11,000 V', and the reveal 'from each foot to the ground' match the code. The reveal quotes the stored across value (0.003 V on the QA path at 7 cm), which the claim allows.

claims.text: With feet on one line, the current through the bird is about 0.2 µA (stage: 'bird 0.2 µA'); with a wing on the grounded pole, 11,000 V is across it and about 1.1 A flows (stage: 'bird 1.1 A', 'to pole 11,000 V'; reveal: 'the difference jumped to 11,000 V').
claims.source: I = ΔV / R with an illustrative bird resistance of 10 kilo-ohm (brief): 0.002 / 10,000 = 2e-7 A; 11,000 / 10,000 = 1.1 A. Arrow width grows with log10 of the current (Demo.tsx comment), so it is a picture of order of magnitude, not a linear scale. Electrocution of birds that bridge a conductor and a grounded pole or two conductors is documented in APLIC, Suggested Practices for Avian Protection on Power Lines (2006) (fact-checker confirms). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node port: birdI = birdV / 10,000: 0.002 V gives 2e-7 A, fmtI '0.2 µA' at the 5 cm default (0.1 to 0.8 µA over 2 to 20 cm, so 'about 0.2 µA' is the default case); wing on gives 11,000 / 10,000 = '1.1 A' and the reading 'to pole 11,000 V'. Reveal 'the difference jumped to 11,000 V' needs the pole milestone. These are in-model derivations from illustrative constants; APLIC (2006), cited for real electrocutions, was not opened and is not relied on.

claims.text: The pole is drawn as grounded (0 V), with the line held off it by an insulator.
claims.source: Distribution poles carry grounded hardware (ground wires, bonded crossarm fittings) and the conductor sits on insulators; APLIC (2006) describes grounded hardware as the electrocution path for perching birds. Stage drawing only (no stage text). Fact-checker confirms the wording. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Convention, checked against the SVG: the pole rect runs into the ground line (GROUND = 176), an insulator rect sits on the crossarm, and the wire starts at the insulator (POLE_X + 27), not on the pole. The wing reading (foot to pole) is V_LINE, i.e. the pole is treated as 0 V. No stage text says 'grounded'; the claim is about the drawing. APLIC was not opened and is not needed for a drawing convention.

claims.text: Never approach real power lines: current can jump across air.
claims.source: High voltages can arc across an air gap: the breakdown field of dry air is about 3 MV/m (any electrostatics text, e.g. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, section 7.5); utility safety guidance keeps people metres from lines. SAFETY WORDING: must be approved by a reader other than its author before publish (W-361 precedent; brief). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD UNVERIFIED. Safety sentence (reveal muted line) is in Demo.tsx exactly as claimed. It rests on air breakdown and utility guidance (OpenStax UP2 7.5, utility safety pages), and none could be opened (DNS failure, proxy 403). Also, the source note says safety wording needs approval by a reader other than its author (W-361 precedent). Left unverified. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED as fact: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, section 7.6 'Equipotential Surfaces and Conductors' (module m58723, raw GitHub, opened) gives the dielectric strength of air as about 3.0 × 10^6 N/C, above which the air is ionised and conducts. So high voltage can jump an air gap. Not my call: the source field says this safety sentence needs approval by a reader other than its author (W-361), and there is no safety review on disk in company/reviews/bird-on-the-wire/. That gate is the safety reviewer's, not mine.

claims.text: Model: the line is drawn at a steady 11,000 V; on an AC line both feet rise and fall together, so the difference between them stays tiny.
claims.source: Brief claim 5. On AC the line-to-ground voltage varies in time, but both feet sit on the same conductor a few cm apart, so their difference is still I(t) R' L, thousandths of a volt. Stated here and in the Demo.tsx header; not on the stage (text budget). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation: both feet sit on the same conductor, so their difference at any instant is I(t) × (series impedance per metre) × L. With the model's 200 A and 0.2 ohm/km this is ≤ 0.002 × √2 V peak at 5 cm, i.e. tiny, while each foot swings with the line. The Demo.tsx header states the steady-voltage simplification. It is not on stage (no stage text), so it is a model note, not a learner sentence.

recall.question: A squirrel sitting on one power line reaches over and touches a second line at a different voltage. Why is that dangerous when sitting on one line was not?
options: Now there is a voltage difference between the two points it touches
Two lines carry twice the current into it
It is no longer insulated by its feet
recall.why: Current flows through something only when its two ends are at different voltages. On one line both feet are at almost the same voltage; two different lines put a large difference across the animal.
